markingScheme.criterion: Quotes at least two of their own results from the Investigation Record — one where the multiplier was less than 1 (product was smaller) and one where it was greater than 1 (product was larger).
markingScheme.accept: Any two genuine values from the student's own Shrink & Grow Machine trials that show the contrast; exact wording not required.
markingScheme.insufficient: A general claim ('it got smaller') with no actual figures quoted from their own rounds.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly states the rule: multiplying by a fraction less than 1 gives a product smaller than the original number, and multiplying by a fraction greater than 1 gives a product larger than the original number.
markingScheme.accept: Any phrasing that conveys both directions of the rule — 'less than 1 shrinks, greater than 1 grows' or equivalent.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains WHY multiplying by a fraction less than 1 gives a smaller answer — e.g. because you are taking only a part of the number, or because the fraction represents less than one whole group.
markingScheme.accept: Any reasoning that goes beyond restating the rule to explain the mechanism: 'you only get a portion', 'it means less than one whole lot of the number', 'half of something is always less than the whole thing'.
markingScheme.insufficient: Restating the rule ('it's smaller because the fraction is less than 1') without explaining why.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that 4/5 is less than 1 and therefore Recipe A uses LESS flour than 20 kg.
markingScheme.accept: '4/5 is less than 1 so it shrinks the 20 kg', '4/5 of 20 is less than 20', or any equivalent.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that 6/5 is greater than 1 and therefore Recipe B uses MORE flour than 20 kg.
markingScheme.accept: '6/5 is more than 1 so it grows the 20 kg', '6/5 of 20 is more than 20', or any equivalent.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains the general method: you can tell which recipe uses more or less just by comparing each fraction to 1 — fractions less than 1 reduce the amount, fractions greater than 1 increase it — without needing to calculate.
markingScheme.accept: Any clear statement that the comparison to 1 is the key, applied to the specific fractions in the question.
markingScheme.insufficient: Calculating 20 × 4/5 = 16 and 20 × 6/5 = 24 without explaining the reasoning about fractions relative to 1.
